title: Slone Site (15Pi11), Pike County
summary: In Pike County, the Slone Site was a Fort Ancient circular village of about 1350–1400 CE, excavated by University of Kentucky crews in 1963–64.
bodyMarkdown:
Around 1350 CE, Fort Ancient farmers in Pike County built a round village behind a wooden wall. They lived there for only thirty to forty-five years. The evidence comes from how many times they rebuilt their houses and the wall. In that time, the village grew so much that its wall had to be moved outward twice.

We know so much about Slone because so much of it was dug. In 1963 and 1964, before a reservoir project flooded the area, University of Kentucky crews excavated about eighty percent of the site. That makes it one of the most complete views of a late Middle [Fort Ancient](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fort_Ancient) village in eastern Kentucky.

The village was laid out in rings. At the center was an open plaza. Around it was a band for cooking and storage, with hearths, earth ovens and storage pits. There was very little trash in this band, so residents probably swept it clean.

Next came the houses, at least twelve of them. On average, each was about 19 by 28 feet, with a hearth in the middle. Behind the houses, families piled their trash: broken jars, broken arrowheads and animal bone. Family cemeteries were also placed behind the homes, keeping relatives close.

A [palisade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Palisade) surrounded everything. The first wall made the village just over 200 feet across. Later, residents took that wall down, built new houses where it had stood, and put up a second wall about 240 feet across. Near the end, a third wall reached about 255 feet.

The walls may have protected the village from attack. They also marked clearly who belonged inside.

Slone is also known for its stone discoidals. Crews found more than 150 of these round stones. Most were sandstone, and a few were made of cannel coal, hematite or limestone. Most were plain and smooth on both sides, and a few were polished or decorated with cut lines.

People probably used them to play [chunkey](https://grokipedia.com/page/Chunkey). In this game, one player rolled the stone across a flat field and players threw spears or shot arrows after it. Whoever landed closest to where the stone stopped scored a point.

## Kentucky today

The village site now lies under water, and its location is protected on this map. What survives is the record from 1963–64 and the collections it produced. In Pike County, Slone shows that walled farming towns were part of mountain life long before the frontier. Its many game stones show that everyday life there also had room for play.
Source: [https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Slone.aspx](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Slone.aspx)
